slides.title: Every claim is tested in code first, then proved
slides.text: Seven weeks Every claim is tested in code first, then proved Test Run the claim on generated cases, or on every case when there are few. A failure is a counterexample. Prove An argument that covers every case, including the ones no test reached. Mind the gap A thousand passing tests prove nothing about the next case. Week 4 shows a claim that fails on its forty-first. Assessed work Weight Weekly problem sets 20% Two supervised AI-off tests of proofs and short problems 40% Capstone portfolio, rubric-scored 30% Oral defence 10%

slides.title: One command proves your setup
slides.text: Setup check One command proves your setup From the course folder, in a terminal: cd labs uv run python -c "import pysat, networkx; print('ready')" "ready" means you can run every lab. In a free hosted notebook, the first cell of each lab installs what it needs. What the course assumes School algebra, and Python with lists, loops, functions and recursion (FND-PRG-101 or equivalent). Nothing of FND-PRG-101 is taught again.

slides.title: All seven weeks work on one community volunteer centre
slides.text: The case All seven weeks work on one community volunteer centre A non-profit in one city: 4,000 volunteers in twelve postal districts, PD-01 to PD-12 It trains them, staffs 30 events a month and runs a nightly data pipeline You are its new data analyst; you work with the volunteer coordinator, the data protection officer and the operations lead Synthetic, and coded Every record is generated with a fixed seed. People appear only as codes such as V-00412: no names, no phone numbers, no real identifiers.

slides.title: Sets, functions and relations
slides.text: Session 1 Sets, functions and relations Compute set operations and the size of a Cartesian product, and check them in code Decide whether a map from the data is a function and whether it is injective, surjective or bijective Compose two relations and explain how a database join differs from the composition 01

slides.title: A set has no order and no repeats, and a table of distinct rows is one
slides.text: Block A · sets A set has no order and no repeats, and a table of distinct rows is one {2, 3, 5} = {5, 3, 2} = {2, 2, 3, 5}: order and repeats do not count x ∈ A reads "x is a member of A"; A ⊆ B, every member of A is in B A row of a table is a tuple: (T3, room 2) is not (room 2, T3) A table with no duplicate rows is a set of tuples A = {2, 3, 5} B = {5, 7} A | B, A & B, A - B # {2, 3, 5, 7}, {5}, {2, 3}

slides.title: Union, intersection and difference answer the coordinator's first questions
slides.text: Operations Union, intersection and difference answer the coordinator's first questions Question Operation Example: X = {a, b, c}, Y = {b, d} Worked at either site X ∪ Y {a, b, c, d} Worked at both X ∩ Y {b} Only at the first X − Y {a, c} How many at either |X ∪ Y| = |X| + |Y| − |X ∩ Y| 3 + 2 − 1 = 4 The last line is inclusion-exclusion for two sets. Week 6 uses it on a whole register.

slides.title: A Cartesian product holds every pair, and its size is the product of the sizes
slides.text: Products A Cartesian product holds every pair, and its size is the product of the sizes {T1, T2} × {room 1, room 2, room 3} = {(T1, room 1), (T1, room 2), (T1, room 3), (T2, room 1), (T2, room 2), (T2, room 3)} |A × B| = |A| · |B| = 2 · 3 = 6 A relation is a subset of a product Any set of pairs from A × B is a relation from A to B. With 6 pairs there are 2⁶ = 64 relations, from the empty one to all of A × B.

slides.title: How many pairs?
slides.text: Checkpoint How many pairs? A training team lists 8 modules and 5 rooms. It wants one row for every module and room that could be booked together. How many rows does that table have? 13 40 2 to the power 40 80

slides.title: A function gives every input exactly one output
slides.text: Block B · functions A function gives every input exactly one output A function from X to Y A relation in which each x in X appears in exactly one pair. X is the domain, Y the codomain. Two ways to fail Some x has no output (the map is partial), or some x has two outputs (the map is not single-valued). Module Room Verdict T1 room 1 fine T2 room 1, room 3 two outputs: not a function T3 (none) no output: partial

slides.title: Injective, surjective and bijective say how outputs are shared and covered
slides.text: Three properties Injective, surjective and bijective say how outputs are shared and covered Injective No two inputs share an output. Test: f(x) = f(x′) forces x = x′. Surjective Every element of the codomain is reached by some input. Bijective Both: a perfect pairing, so the map has an inverse. On the integers. n ↦ 3n is injective and not surjective (5 is never reached); n ↦ n − 7 is a bijection.

slides.title: Each property is a promise a system relies on
slides.text: In data work Each property is a promise a system relies on Property Where a system relies on it Function (total) Every record finds its value in a lookup Injective A key or a code identifies one record: no two people check in as one Surjective Every category is used: every event has staff Bijective A code can be swapped back for the record: pseudonymisation, week 6

slides.title: What kind of map is this?
slides.text: Checkpoint What kind of map is this? A sports hall gives each of its 120 lockers to one of 4 cleaning rounds, every round gets 30 lockers. As a map from lockers to rounds, which is true? A bijection, since every round gets the same number Not a function, since each round has many lockers Injective, since every round is used A surjective function that is not injective

slides.title: Equivalences group things; orders rank them
slides.text: Block C · relations Equivalences group things; orders rank them Equivalence relation Reflexive, symmetric and transitive. "Lives in the same district as" splits people into groups, the equivalence classes. Partial order Reflexive, antisymmetric and transitive. "Must be taken before, directly or through others, or is the same module as" ranks modules; some pairs are not comparable. Reflexive: every x relates to itself. Symmetric: x R y gives y R x Transitive: x R y and y R z give x R z. Antisymmetric: x R y and y R x give x = y

slides.title: Composing two relations follows one, then the other
slides.text: Composition Composing two relations follows one, then the other R: module → room (T1, r1), (T2, r1), (T3, r2) → S: room → building (r1, North), (r2, South), (r2, Annex) → R then S (T1, North), (T2, North), (T3, South), (T3, Annex) (x, z) is in the composition when some y has (x, y) in R and (y, z) in S.

slides.title: A join is a composition that keeps repeats
slides.text: In a database A join is a composition that keeps repeats select r.module, s.building from R r join S s on r.room = s.room One output row per pair of matching rows If T2 used room 1 twice (two bookings), (T2, North) appears twice select distinct returns the composition, a set What goes wrong. Counting join rows as "modules per building" overcounts by every repeat. The lab measures how many.

slides.title: Join rows or composition pairs?
slides.text: Checkpoint Join rows or composition pairs? A library joins loans (reader, copy) with copies (copy, title). One reader borrowed two copies of the same title. Compared with the composition "reader borrowed title", the join returns: the same number of rows as there are pairs one fewer row, as the second copy is dropped one more row: the (reader, title) pair appears twice an error, as the key repeats

W1_1.ipynb Set up and load the centre's tables 10 min Set operations and Cartesian products, by hand and in code 10 min Is the badge map a function? Total, injective, surjective 20 min Shift to event: a function onto the events? 10 min Inverse and composition of relations 15 min Compose assignments with shifts, then join them in SQL 20 min Record what the coordinator should fix 5 min ✱ Stretch: Show on the three tables that composing relations is associative

slides.text: Debrief · lab 1.1 The badge map fails all three tests, and the join overcounts by eight Check Result Function on the 300 volunteers no: V-00117 and V-00242 have no badge Injective no: BD-0059, BD-0420, BD-0909 issued twice Shift to event a function onto the 30 events, 3 shifts each Join rows against composition 600 rows, 592 distinct pairs V-00117 is also on a shift: fix before the event Eight volunteers work two shifts of one event Count events per volunteer with distinct pairs

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Week 1 · wrap-up Three things to keep Tables are sets of tuples Products count the possible rows; relations are subsets of them. Functions make promises Total, single-valued, injective, surjective: check each one; data breaks them quietly. Joins compose relations With repeats. Distinct pairs are the composition.

slides.title: Can the code be swapped back?
slides.text: Review · week 1 Can the code be swapped back? A school replaces each of its 500 pupil numbers with a random code from 1,000 possible codes, never giving one code twice. As a map from pupils to the 1,000 codes, what is it? A bijection Injective, not surjective Surjective, not injective Not a function

slides.title: Propositional logic, normal forms and SAT
slides.text: Session 1 Propositional logic, normal forms and SAT Translate a plain-language rule into a propositional formula and check it by truth table Distinguish a valid argument from an invalid one by searching for a counterexample row Encode a small scheduling problem in conjunctive normal form and solve it with a SAT solver 01

slides.title: A proposition is true or false, and connectives build bigger ones
slides.text: Block A · propositions A proposition is true or false, and connectives build bigger ones Symbol Reads True when ¬p not p p is false p ∧ q p and q both are true p ∨ q p or q at least one is true p → q if p then q p is false, or q is true p ↔ q p if and only if q both have the same value

slides.title: "If p then q" is broken only by p true and q false
slides.text: Implication "If p then q" is broken only by p true and q false p: over 20 kg q: two lifters p → q F F T F T T T F F T T T A light parcel lifted by two people does not break the rule A light parcel makes the rule true whatever happens: vacuously Only a heavy parcel lifted alone breaks it

slides.title: A truth table is a loop over every row of truth values
slides.text: In code A truth table is a loop over every row of truth values import itertools def implies(a, b): return (not a) or b for p, q in itertools.product([False, True], repeat=2): print(p, q, implies(p, q)) n variables give 2ⁿ rows: 4 for two, 1,024 for ten Checking every row is a proof for a finite claim For 50 variables, 2⁵⁰ rows is out of reach: that is where a solver comes in

slides.title: Two formulas are equivalent when they agree on every row
slides.text: Equivalence Two formulas are equivalent when they agree on every row Law Equivalent pair De Morgan ¬(p ∧ q) and ¬p ∨ ¬q; ¬(p ∨ q) and ¬p ∧ ¬q Contrapositive p → q and ¬q → ¬p Implication as or p → q and ¬p ∨ q Distribution p ∧ (q ∨ r) and (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r) Not a law. The converse q → p is a different rule: a parcel lifted by two people need not be heavy.

slides.title: Which sentence says the same thing?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which sentence says the same thing? A warehouse rule: "If a box is fragile, it is packed with foam." Which sentence is equivalent to it? If a box is packed with foam, it is fragile If a box is not fragile, it is not packed with foam Every box is fragile and packed with foam If a box is not packed with foam, it is not fragile

slides.title: An argument is valid when no row makes the premises true and the conclusion false
slides.text: Block B · arguments An argument is valid when no row makes the premises true and the conclusion false Form Premises Conclusion Verdict Modus ponens p → q, p q valid Modus tollens p → q, ¬q ¬p valid Affirming the consequent p → q, q p invalid: row p F, q T Denying the antecedent p → q, ¬p ¬q invalid: row p F, q T Validity is about form, not truth: a valid argument from a false premise can reach a false conclusion.

slides.title: Words like "only if" and "unless" fix the direction of the arrow
slides.text: Rules in words Words like "only if" and "unless" fix the direction of the arrow Words Formula p if q q → p p only if q p → q p unless q ¬q → p, the same as p ∨ q A or B and C ambiguous: (A ∨ B) ∧ C, or A ∨ (B ∧ C) Habit. Name each variable in one line, write the formula with brackets, then read it back in words.

slides.title: Translate the rule
slides.text: Checkpoint Translate the rule A laboratory: "A visitor may enter only if they wear goggles." With p = "the visitor enters" and s = "the visitor wears goggles", which formula is the rule? s → p p → s p ∧ s p ↔ s

slides.title: Conjunctive normal form is an "and" of clauses, each an "or" of literals
slides.text: Block C · normal form Conjunctive normal form is an "and" of clauses, each an "or" of literals (a ∨ b) ∧ (¬a ∨ c) ∧ (¬b ∨ ¬c) A literal is a variable or its negation A clause is an or of literals: at least one must hold Every formula has an equivalent CNF: one clause per row it must exclude For a solver Variables are numbers and a clause is a list: [1, 2], [-1, 3], [-2, -3]. A minus sign is "not".

slides.title: A SAT solver finds a row that makes every clause true, or proves there is none
slides.text: Satisfiability A SAT solver finds a row that makes every clause true, or proves there is none Encode one variable per yes-or-no decision; one clause per rule → Solve a model: a value for every variable, or "unsatisfiable" → Check the model against the rules in words, with separate code Checking a proposed assignment is quick; finding one can take exponential time in the worst case with every known method "Unsatisfiable" is a proof that no assignment works; a solver can name a small set of rules that already conflict

slides.title: "Exactly one" and "at most two" become many small clauses
slides.text: Encoding "Exactly one" and "at most two" become many small clauses Rule over n yes-or-no variables Clauses For n = 8 At least one 1 clause of n literals 1 At most one: no two together one per pair, n(n − 1)/2 28 At most two: no three together one per triple, n(n − 1)(n − 2)/6 56 At least two: someone besides each one n clauses of n − 1 literals 8

slides.title: What does "unsatisfiable" tell the planner?
slides.text: Checkpoint What does "unsatisfiable" tell the planner? A clinic encodes its nurse rota and the solver answers "unsatisfiable". What has been established? The solver failed and should be run again with more time No rota was found among those the solver tried No rota meets all the clauses as written No rota meets the clinic's real rules

W2_1.ipynb Set up; a truth table by hand and in code 15 min Equivalent or not: laws by truth table 15 min Valid and invalid arguments 15 min Two phrasings of an access rule 15 min Encode the shift puzzle in CNF 20 min Solve, then check against every rule 10 min The late change: unsatisfiable, and why 10 min Small variant: brute force against solver 5 min ✱ Stretch: Count every schedule of the full puzzle by blocking each one found

slides.text: Debrief · lab 2.1 The handbook opens contact details to anyone, for consenting volunteers Result Value Rows where the two phrasings differ 2 of 16: o F, c F, s T Shift puzzle 50 variables, 800 clauses, a schedule found and checked After the late change unsatisfiable: one first-aider for SH-C and SH-D Small variant 36 schedules by brute force, by solver and by 3! · 3! slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Week 2 · wrap-up Three things to keep Only one row breaks "if" p true and q false. The converse is a different rule. Validity is a row search Look for premises true and conclusion false. None found in every row: valid. Encode, solve, check A solver meets the clauses you wrote. Check its answer against the words.

slides.text: SDAIA Academy · Discrete Mathematics and Logic for Computing Predicates, quantifiers and first proofs Week 3: Properties of relations stated with quantifiers, checked on data, then proved or refuted Data & AI Foundations Track7 weeks + capstone1 session · 1 labFND-MTH-105

slides.title: Predicates, quantifiers and first proofs
slides.text: This week Predicates, quantifiers and first proofs Session 1 · Quantifiers, relations and first proofs Predicates and quantifiers, the properties of relations, equivalence relations and orders, and direct proof, counterexample and contradiction

slides.title: Valid or not?
slides.text: Review · week 2 Valid or not? Rule: if a meter reading is missing, the bill is estimated. This bill is not estimated. What follows? The reading is not missing The reading is missing Nothing: the rule says nothing about estimated bills The bill would be estimated if the reading were present

slides.title: Quantifiers, relations and first proofs
slides.text: Session 1 Quantifiers, relations and first proofs Write a relation property or a data-quality rule with quantifiers and negate it correctly Classify a relation as a function, an equivalence, a partial order or none, with a counterexample for each property it lacks Prove a short claim directly or by contradiction, and refute a false one with a counterexample 01

slides.title: A predicate becomes true or false once you fill its variable
slides.text: Block A · quantifiers A predicate becomes true or false once you fill its variable P(x) : "x is overdue", over a domain such as the loans of a library ∀x P(x) : every loan is overdue ∃x P(x) : at least one loan is overdue The domain is part of the claim: change it and the truth can change all(overdue(x) for x in loans) # for every any(overdue(x) for x in loans) # there exists

slides.title: A data-quality rule is a quantified statement your code can evaluate
slides.text: Data-quality rules A data-quality rule is a quantified statement your code can evaluate Rule in words In logic Every loan belongs to a member ∀l ∃m: holder(l, m) No member holds more than five loans ∀m: count of l with holder(l, m) ≤ 5 Every child member has a guardian on file ∀m: child(m) → guardian(m) A failed rule comes with a witness: the loan with no member, the child with no guardian. Print the witness, not only "False".

slides.title: Negating a quantifier swaps it and moves the "not" inside
slides.text: Negation Negating a quantifier swaps it and moves the "not" inside Statement Its negation ∀x P(x): every loan is returned ∃x ¬P(x): some loan is not returned ∃x P(x): some book is damaged ∀x ¬P(x): no book is damaged ∀x ∃y R(x, y): every member has a card ∃x ∀y ¬R(x, y): some member has no card at all Order matters. ∀x ∃y "every member has a card" is not ∃y ∀x "one card belongs to every member".

slides.title: What is the negation?
slides.text: Checkpoint What is the negation? The claim: "every course has at least one tutor". Which statement is its negation? Every course has no tutor Some course has at least one tutor Some course has no tutor One tutor teaches no course

slides.title: Each property of a relation is a "for every" statement
slides.text: Block B · relation properties Each property of a relation is a "for every" statement Property Statement A counterexample is Reflexive ∀x: x R x one x not related to itself Symmetric ∀x, y: x R y → y R x one pair related one way only Antisymmetric ∀x, y: x R y ∧ y R x → x = y two different elements related both ways Transitive ∀x, y, z: x R y ∧ y R z → x R z one chain x, y, z with x not related to z

slides.title: The properties decide what a relation can be used for
slides.text: Kinds of relation The properties decide what a relation can be used for Kind Properties Example Equivalence refl, sym, trans born in the same month Partial order refl, anti, trans is a subset of Strict order irrefl, anti, trans finished earlier than Preorder refl, trans is at least as tall as Group with an equivalence Rank or schedule with an order A preorder ranks with ties between different elements

slides.title: On a finite relation, checking every case is a proof
slides.text: Testing or proving On a finite relation, checking every case is a proof Finite: check them all "Same month" on 40 people: 1,600 pairs and 64,000 triples. Checking them all proves the property for those 40. Infinite: test, then prove "Subset of" on all sets, "divides" on all integers: no loop ends. Tests can refute; only an argument proves. Mind the definition. If a relation is defined by a rule ("within 5 km"), a property may fail for the next element even when it holds for today's data.

slides.title: Can it be used to form groups?
slides.text: Checkpoint Can it be used to form groups? A delivery firm relates two depots when they are within 5 km of each other, and wants to form groups of "nearby" depots with it. What is this relation? An equivalence relation, so the groups are well defined Reflexive and symmetric, not transitive, so not an equivalence A partial order on the depots Symmetric only, as no depot relates to itself

slides.title: A direct proof goes from the hypothesis to the conclusion, one justified step at a time
slides.text: Block C · proofs A direct proof goes from the hypothesis to the conclusion, one justified step at a time Claim. The sum of two even integers is even. Let a and b be even: a = 2k and b = 2l for integers k, l (definition) a + b = 2k + 2l = 2(k + l) (algebra) k + l is an integer, so a + b is even (definition) ∎ The shape State the claim with its domain. Unfold the definitions. Calculate. Fold back into the definition of the conclusion. Name each reason.

slides.title: One counterexample refutes a "for every" claim
slides.text: Refuting One counterexample refutes a "for every" claim Claim Counterexample Every prime is odd 2 If a² = b² then a = b, for integers a = 3, b = −3 n² − n + 11 is prime for every n ≥ 1 n = 11: 121 = 11 · 11 The last claim holds for n = 1 to 10. Code finds the counterexample in a moment; a person checking by hand may stop too early.

slides.title: A proof by contradiction assumes the opposite and reaches something impossible
slides.text: Contradiction A proof by contradiction assumes the opposite and reaches something impossible Claim. If n² is even, then n is even (n an integer). Suppose n² is even and n is odd: n = 2k + 1 n² = 4k² + 4k + 1 = 2(2k² + 2k) + 1, which is odd n² is both even and odd: impossible. So n is even ∎ Say what you assumed The first line names the assumption; the last names the contradiction. A reader can then check that the assumption really is the negation of the claim.

slides.title: What settles the claim?
slides.text: Checkpoint What settles the claim? An analyst claims: "for every integer n, n² + n is even". Her code checks n from −1,000 to 1,000 and finds no failure. What has she shown? That the claim is true, since 2,001 cases passed Nothing: tests are no evidence either way That the claim is false for some large n No counterexample in that range; a proof is still needed

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Week 3 · wrap-up Three things to keep Negate carefully Swap ∀ and ∃ and move the "not" inside. The negation tells you what a counterexample looks like. Properties decide use Group only with an equivalence; rank only with an order. Check before you use. Finite or infinite Every case checked is a proof for a finite set. For the integers, tests refute and proofs prove.

slides.title: Which property fails?
slides.text: Review · week 3 Which property fails? On the files of a shared drive, "file A is in the same folder as file B or in one of its subfolders" relates A to B. Which property does it lack? Reflexivity Transitivity It has all four, so it is an equivalence Symmetry

slides.title: Induction, invariants, testing and proof
slides.text: Session 1 Induction, invariants, testing and proof Prove a claim about the integers by mathematical induction after testing it in code Prove a property of a recursive structure by structural induction State and check a loop invariant, and use it to prove a loop correct 01

slides.title: Induction proves a claim for every n with two finite pieces of work
slides.text: Block A · induction Induction proves a claim for every n with two finite pieces of work Base show P(1), or P of the first value → Hypothesis assume P(k) for one k ≥ 1 → Step show P(k + 1), using P(k) Base and step together reach every n: P(1), so P(2), so P(3), and so on Without the base, the step proves nothing; without the step, the base proves one case

slides.title: Test it, then prove it: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1) / 2
slides.text: Worked example Test it, then prove it: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1) / 2 all(sum(range(1, n + 1)) == n * (n + 1) // 2 for n in range(1, 5001)) # True Base. n = 1: 1 = 1 · 2 / 2 Hypothesis. 1 + … + k = k(k + 1) / 2 Step. 1 + … + k + (k + 1) = k(k + 1) / 2 + (k + 1) = (k + 1)(k + 2) / 2, using the hypothesis for the first k terms ∎

slides.title: Strong induction may assume the claim for every value below k + 1
slides.text: Strong induction Strong induction may assume the claim for every value below k + 1 Claim. Every integer n ≥ 2 is a product of primes. If n is prime, it is a product of one prime Otherwise n = a · b with 2 ≤ a, b < n By the hypothesis for a and for b, both are products of primes, so n is too ∎ When to use it When the step needs a smaller case that is not k itself: a factor, half of n, a subtree. Recursive code that splits its input is proved this way.

slides.title: What is missing?
slides.text: Checkpoint What is missing? A proof that "n + 1 < n for every n ≥ 1" assumes k + 1 < k and adds 1 to both sides to get k + 2 < k + 1. What is wrong with it? It has no base case, and the base case is false Adding 1 to both sides is not allowed The hypothesis assumes what it wants to prove It needs strong induction instead

slides.title: Structural induction follows the way a structure is built
slides.text: Block B · structural induction Structural induction follows the way a structure is built A recursive definition A nested list is either a number, or a list of nested lists. A tree is a node with a list of subtrees. Its induction Prove the claim for the smallest pieces, then show that building from pieces that satisfy it gives a whole that satisfies it. No n needed. The induction is on the structure itself; each recursive call works on a smaller part.

slides.title: In a tree where every node has 0 or 2 children, leaves = inner nodes + 1
slides.text: Worked example In a tree where every node has 0 or 2 children, leaves = inner nodes + 1 Base. A single node: 1 leaf, 0 inner nodes Step. A root with subtrees L and R that satisfy it: leaves = (inner(L) + 1) + (inner(R) + 1) = (inner(L) + inner(R) + 1) + 1 The root is the one new inner node, so leaves = inner + 1 ∎ def leaves(t): if not t["children"]: return 1 return sum(leaves(c) for c in t["children"])

slides.title: A recursive function is proved correct by induction on the size of its input
slides.text: Recursive code A recursive function is proved correct by induction on the size of its input def total(xs): if not xs: return 0 return xs[0] + total(xs[1:]) Base. The empty list returns 0, its sum Hypothesis. total is right on lists of length k Step. On length k + 1 it returns xs[0] plus the sum of the rest, by the hypothesis: the sum ∎

slides.title: What may the step assume?
slides.text: Checkpoint What may the step assume? To prove by structural induction that a recursive depth function on nested lists is correct, the step for a list [a, b, c] may assume: that the function is correct on [a, b, c] that it is correct on a only that it is correct on each of a, b and c that it is correct on every list of length 2

slides.title: An invariant is true before the loop and after every pass
slides.text: Block C · loop invariants An invariant is true before the loop and after every pass total, i = 0, 0 while i < len(xs): # invariant: total == sum(xs[:i]) total += xs[i] i += 1 Part Show Initialisation true before the first pass Maintenance a pass keeps it true Termination the loop stops At exit invariant and exit condition give the result

slides.title: A pattern can hold for every case you tried and still break
slides.text: The gap A pattern can hold for every case you tried and still break Points on a circle Regions 1 1 2 2 3 4 4 8 5 16 6 31 Join every pair of points with a chord, no three chords meeting inside The first five suggest 2ⁿ⁻¹; the sixth gives 31, not 32 A test can refute a pattern; only a proof can confirm it

slides.title: Generated tests find counterexamples cheaply, so run them before you prove
slides.text: Using tests well Generated tests find counterexamples cheaply, so run them before you prove Many cases Every n up to a bound, or random inputs. Cheap evidence and a fast way to find a false claim. Edge cases Zero, one, the empty list, equal values, the first case where a pattern could change. Their limit Write what the tests cover: "n from 1 to 1,000, no counterexample". Never write "true".

slides.title: Which statement is an invariant?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which statement is an invariant? A loop counts the even numbers in a list: count starts at 0, i at 0; each pass adds 1 to count if xs[i] is even, then adds 1 to i. Which invariant proves it correct? count ≥ 0 count equals the number of evens in the whole list count = i count equals the number of evens in xs[:i]

slides.title: Claims tested in code, then proved
slides.text: Lab 4.1 · 105 min Claims tested in code, then proved An added lab: test claims on generated cases, prove them by induction and invariants, and find the gap in a flawed proof. W4_1.ipynb Set up; test a sum formula on many cases 10 min Prove it by induction 15 min True for forty cases, false on the next 10 min Structural induction on the team tree 20 min Loop invariants asserted in code 20 min Find the gap in a flawed proof 15 min Record which claims are proved 15 min ✱ Stretch: Prove an invariant for binary search over the volunteer codes

slides.title: Forty passes did not make claim B true, and one hidden assumption broke a proof
slides.text: Debrief · lab 4.1 Forty passes did not make claim B true, and one hidden assumption broke a proof Claim Status Sum of first n odd numbers is n² tested to 1,000, proved n² + n + 41 is prime passes n = 0 to 39; at 40: 1,681 = 41 · 41 Edges = nodes − 1 team tree 25 and 24; 500 trees; proved divide(a, b) 2,000 pairs; proved from its invariant 2ⁿ ≥ n² for n ≥ 1 fails at n = 3; step needs k ≥ 3 The flawed step used k² ≥ 2k + 1, false for k = 1 and 2 Repaired: 2ⁿ ≥ n² for every n ≥ 4

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Week 4 · wrap-up Three things to keep Base, hypothesis, step Say where the step uses the hypothesis. A step alone proves nothing. Induction follows structure Integers, lists, trees and loops: the proof follows the way the thing is built. Tests refute, proofs confirm Write what your tests cover, never "true", until the proof exists.

slides.title: Counting, collisions and the birthday problem
slides.text: This week Counting, collisions and the birthday problem Session 1 · Counting arrangements and collisions The sum and product rules, permutations and combinations, the pigeonhole principle and collisions of short codes

slides.title: Where is the hypothesis used?
slides.text: Review · week 4 Where is the hypothesis used? To prove 1 + 3 + 9 + … + 3ⁿ⁻¹ = (3ⁿ − 1) / 2 by induction, the step for k + 1 must: check the formula for n = k + 1 by computing both sides for k = 5 assume the formula for k + 1 and simplify replace the first k terms by (3ᵏ − 1) / 2, add 3ᵏ, and simplify to (3ᵏ⁺¹ − 1) / 2 test the formula for n up to 1,000

slides.title: Counting arrangements and collisions
slides.text: Session 1 Counting arrangements and collisions Count arrangements and selections with the sum and product rules, permutations and combinations Compute the chance that short codes collide and verify it by exact enumeration Use the pigeonhole principle to show when a collision is certain 01

slides.title: Multiply for "and then", add for "either, or"
slides.text: Block A · two rules Multiply for "and then", add for "either, or" Product rule A plate of 3 letters then 4 digits: 26 · 26 · 26 · 10 · 10 · 10 · 10 = 175,760,000 plates. Sum rule A PIN of 4, 5 or 6 digits: 10⁴ + 10⁵ + 10⁶ = 1,110,000 PINs. The three lengths never overlap. The sum rule needs disjoint cases. When cases overlap, subtract what was counted twice: inclusion-exclusion, week 6.

slides.title: Order matters in an arrangement, not in a selection
slides.text: Arrangements and selections Order matters in an arrangement, not in a selection Question, from 8 people Formula Count Chair, deputy and secretary P(8, 3) = 8 · 7 · 6 336 A committee of 3 C(8, 3) = P(8, 3) / 3! 56 Why divide by 3! each committee can be ordered in 3! = 6 ways P(n, k) = n! / (n − k)! and C(n, k) = n! / (k! (n − k)!).

slides.title: Arrangement or selection?
slides.text: Checkpoint Arrangement or selection? A tasting panel of 4 judges is chosen from 9 cooks; the judges have no roles. How many panels are possible? 3,024 126 6,561 36

slides.title: All-different assignments are an arrangement count
slides.text: Block B · collisions All-different assignments are an arrangement count n people, each given one of N codes: Nⁿ assignments All codes different: N (N − 1) … (N − n + 1) = P(N, n) Chance all different = P(N, n) / Nⁿ, a count divided by a count Checked by listing 6 codes, 3 people: listing all 216 assignments finds 120 with no repeat, and 6 · 5 · 4 = 120. The chance is 120 / 216 = 5/9.

slides.title: With 100 codes, 13 people already share one more often than not
slides.text: The birthday effect With 100 codes, 13 people already share one more often than not 5 people 9.65% 10 people 37.18% 13 people 55.72% 20 people 86.96% Exact chance of a shared code among n people with 100 equally likely codes.

slides.title: The average number of colliding pairs is C(n, 2) / N
slides.text: Pairs The average number of colliding pairs is C(n, 2) / N Each of the C(n, 2) pairs shares a code in N · Nⁿ⁻² of the Nⁿ assignments So, averaged over all assignments, a pair collides 1/N of the time 30 people, 100 codes: C(30, 2) / 100 = 4.35 colliding pairs on average A count, not a simulation The average is a total over every assignment divided by their number. Brute force on small cases checks it exactly.

slides.title: How many colliding pairs to expect?
slides.text: Checkpoint How many colliding pairs to expect? A shop gives each of 50 loyalty cards a random 3-digit code (1,000 codes). On average over all assignments, how many pairs of cards share a code? 0.05 2.45 50 1.225

slides.title: More items than boxes means some box holds two, and ⌈n / N⌉ is guaranteed
slides.text: Block C · pigeonhole More items than boxes means some box holds two, and ⌈n / N⌉ is guaranteed 1,000 people and 366 possible birthdays: some day holds at least ⌈1000 / 366⌉ = 3 people Proof by contradiction: if every box held at most ⌈n / N⌉ − 1, the boxes would hold fewer than n items Below n = N, nothing is guaranteed, though collisions may be likely In hashing Any map from long codes to short codes squeezes many inputs into each output: collisions are certain, only their rate is in question.

slides.title: Choose a code length from the risk you accept, not from the number of people
slides.text: Design Choose a code length from the risk you accept, not from the number of people State the risk "at most 1 in 100 that any two share a code" → Compute exactly the chance for each length, with the formula → Plan for the rest a second check when a collision still happens What goes wrong. "We have 4,000 people and 65,536 codes, so codes are plenty" ignores the pairs. The lab measures how wrong that is.

slides.title: What is guaranteed?
slides.text: Checkpoint What is guaranteed? A depot sorts 830 parcels into 100 bays by the last two digits of the parcel number. What does the pigeonhole principle guarantee? Some bay receives at least 9 parcels Every bay receives 8 or 9 parcels Some bay receives at least 8 parcels, and no more is guaranteed Nothing, since 830 is less than 100 · 100

slides.text: Lab 5.1 · 105 min Hash collisions and the birthday problem, by formula and by brute force Cut check-in codes from a hash, count collisions two ways, and choose a code length. W5_1.ipynb Set up; sum and product rules 10 min Arrangements and selections, two ways 15 min Short check-in codes from a hash 10 min Collision-free count: formula and brute force 20 min The birthday problem exactly, with fractions 15 min Expected colliding pairs against those issued 15 min Pigeonhole: when a collision is certain 10 min Choose the code length and record it 10 min ✱ Stretch: Count the shared birthdays in the register and compare with the formula

slides.text: Debrief · lab 5.1 Four symbols leave 125 colliding pairs; the centre needs eight k Codes Expected pairs Counted 3 4,096 1,952.6 2,026 4 65,536 122.0 125 5 1,048,576 7.6 6 6 16,777,216 0.5 1 Birthdays: 23 people pass one half; four symbols: 302 codes k = 2: at least 16 share a code; the largest group found is 27 1% risk: k = 8 for 4,000 (0.19%), k = 10 for 40,000

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Week 5 · wrap-up Three things to keep Multiply, add, divide Product for steps, sum for disjoint cases, divide by the orderings you do not want. Pairs drive collisions C(n, 2) / N pairs on average; trouble starts near the square root of N. Check counts by listing Brute force on small cases catches the errors a formula hides.

slides.title: Counting people: re-identification risk
slides.text: This week Counting people: re-identification risk Session 1 · Inclusion-exclusion and linkage risk Inclusion-exclusion, the product rule over quasi-identifiers, class sizes in a register, generalisation, and personal versus anonymised data

slides.title: How many all-different assignments?
slides.text: Review · week 5 How many all-different assignments? Five interns each draw one of 8 desk numbers. In how many of the 8⁵ draws do all five get different desks? 56 32,768 6,720 40,320

slides.title: Inclusion-exclusion and linkage risk
slides.text: Session 1 Inclusion-exclusion and linkage risk Count the people who share each combination of quasi-identifiers and find who is unique Apply inclusion-exclusion to count records that meet at least one of several conditions, and check it with sets Explain why removing the direct identifier does not anonymise data, and what generalisation changes 01

slides.title: Add the sets, then subtract what you counted twice
slides.text: Block A · inclusion-exclusion Add the sets, then subtract what you counted twice |A ∪ B| = |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| |A| = 60, |B| = 50, |A ∩ B| = 20: |A ∪ B| = 90. Three sets: |A ∪ B ∪ C| = |A| + |B| + |C| − |A ∩ B| − |A ∩ C| − |B ∩ C| + |A ∩ B ∩ C| Why it works An element in exactly two of three sets is added twice and subtracted once; one in all three is added three times, subtracted three times, added once. Every element ends with count 1.

slides.title: A formula over counts can be checked against the sets themselves
slides.text: Checked with sets A formula over counts can be checked against the sets themselves ie = len(A) + len(B) - len(A & B) assert ie == len(A | B) The formula needs only counts: useful when the sets are held by different teams The union needs the elements themselves On data you hold, compute both: they must agree

slides.title: How many are in at least one?
slides.text: Checkpoint How many are in at least one? Of a club's members, 45 read the newsletter, 30 attend events and 12 do both. How many do at least one of the two? 75 63 51 33

slides.title: Quasi-identifiers single people out in combination
slides.text: Block B · counting people Quasi-identifiers single people out in combination Direct identifier Identifies a person alone: a name, a member number, a code assigned to one person. "Removing names" removes these columns. Quasi-identifiers Shared by many people alone, but rare in combination: birth date, sex, postal district. Often known to neighbours and colleagues. The question to count. After the direct identifiers are gone, how many people are alone in their combination of quasi-identifiers?

slides.title: When combinations outnumber people, almost everyone is unique
slides.text: The product rule again When combinations outnumber people, almost everyone is unique A town of 20,000 adults, 10 districts Combinations People each Birth date (60 years), sex, district 438,000 0.05 Birth year, sex, district 1,200 16.67 10-year band, sex, district 120 166.67 If people spread evenly, n (1 − 1/M)ⁿ⁻¹ of them are alone among M combinations: 95.5% in the first row.

slides.title: Count the people in each combination, then the people alone
slides.text: By hand first Count the people in each combination, then the people alone Six members: year, sex, area People 1990, F, D1 2 1990, M, D1 1 1985, F, D2 2 1972, M, D3 1 A combination held by one person is a class of size 1 The smallest class says how alone the most exposed people are A release rule can set a smallest class, for example five

slides.title: What does the product rule predict?
slides.text: Checkpoint What does the product rule predict? A survey of 500 people keeps age in years (60 values), sex and one of 4 regions. Roughly how many combinations are there per person? 240,000 66 about 0.48 about 0.96

slides.title: Data that can identify a person indirectly is personal data
slides.text: Block C · the law Data that can identify a person indirectly is personal data Personal Data Protection Law, Article 1 Personal data includes data that "may directly or indirectly make it possible to identify an individual" (SDAIA's English text). SDAIA's anonymisation guideline Anonymised data "shall no longer be considered personal data"; the guideline asks that it be irreversible, with an assessment of re-identification. It states that it is not a binding legal document. So. An extract in which birth date, sex and district single people out still makes identification indirectly possible: removing the code column does not anonymise it.

slides.title: Coarser columns make classes bigger and lose detail
slides.text: Generalisation Coarser columns make classes bigger and lose detail Birth date 438,000 combinations in the parallel town → Birth year 1,200 → 10-year band 120 The guideline's examples include age bands and birth year in place of the full date Each step trades analysis detail for larger classes: say what the analysis loses

slides.title: Releases combine: the risk is the union, not the safer of the two
slides.text: Linkage Releases combine: the risk is the union, not the safer of the two Two tables, each with few people alone, are released: A and B are the people alone in each Anyone in A ∪ B can be found: |A| + |B| − |A ∩ B| people A list published elsewhere with the same columns links back row by row Count before you publish For each row of a list to be posted, count how many people in your register share its quasi-identifiers. One means that row names a person.

slides.title: Is it anonymised?
slides.text: Checkpoint Is it anonymised? A gym removes member numbers from its list and keeps full birth date, sex and home district. Most members are alone in their combination. Under the Law's definition, the list is: anonymised, since no identifier remains still personal data, since it makes identification indirectly possible pseudonymised, so outside the Law personal data only if more than half are unique

slides.text: Lab 6.1 · 105 min Re-identification risk counted from birth date, sex and postal district in a synthetic register Count who shares each combination of birth date, sex and district, generalise, and link a posted sheet back. W6_1.ipynb Set up; the extract without the volunteer code 10 min People per combination of the three columns 15 min Product rule: combinations and expected uniques 15 min Generalise: birth year, five-year bands, district groups 20 min Inclusion-exclusion, checked with sets 15 min Link the posted sign-in sheet 15 min Record for the data protection officer 15 min ✱ Stretch: Find the most detailed release in which every combination holds five people

slides.text: Debrief · lab 6.1 Without its codes, the register still singles out 98.9% of volunteers Release Unique Smallest class Date, sex, district 3,956 1 Year, sex, district 245 1 5-year band, sex, district 19 1 5-year band, sex, district group 6 1 10-year band, sex, district group 0 8 Even spread predicts 3,966 unique; by year it predicts 193, against 245 counted Three tables, each modest alone: 572 people unique in at least one The posted sign-in sheet: all 60 rows match exactly one volunteer

slides.title: Three things to keep
slides.text: Week 6 · wrap-up Three things to keep Subtract the overlap Inclusion-exclusion counts a union from its parts, and code can check it. Count who is alone Removing the identifier column leaves quasi-identifiers; count the classes of size 1. Releases add up Two safe-looking tables, or a posted list, can name people together.

slides.title: How many people can be found?
slides.text: Review · week 6 How many people can be found? Two tables are released. 32 people are alone in their combination in the first, 18 in the second, and 7 of them are alone in both. How many people are alone in at least one table? 43 50 32 36

slides.title: Graphs, cycles, orders and recurrences
slides.text: Session 1 Graphs, cycles, orders and recurrences Model dependencies as a directed graph and decide whether it has a cycle Compute a topological order and check that every edge points forward Set up a recurrence for a count, solve it, and compare how fast functions grow 01

slides.title: A directed graph is a set of nodes and a relation on them
slides.text: Block A · graphs A directed graph is a set of nodes and a relation on them An edge (u, v) is a pair in the relation: here "u must finish before v starts" In-degree : edges arriving; out-degree: edges leaving A source has in-degree 0; a sink has out-degree 0 A path follows edges forward; a cycle is a path that returns to its start A DAG is a directed graph with no cycle; a tree has no cycle even with edges read both ways A morning of five tasks A and B feed C; C feeds D and E. Sources A, B; sinks D, E. The in-degrees add up to 4, the number of edges.

slides.title: A cycle of dependencies means no job on it can ever start
slides.text: Why cycles matter A cycle of dependencies means no job on it can ever start 1 · Start what is ready Every job whose dependencies have all finished → 2 · Peel it off Remove it; its successors lose one unfinished dependency → 3 · Repeat or stop All gone: no cycle. Some left, none ready: a cycle among them Takeaway. In a graph with no cycle there is always a job with nothing unfinished before it, so peeling only stops early when a cycle exists.

slides.title: Which jobs are never ready?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which jobs are never ready? Edges: A → B, B → C, C → D, D → B, A → E. Peeling starts with every job that has no dependency. Which jobs are never ready? B, C and D D only B, C, D and E none, since A has no dependency

slides.title: A topological order puts every edge forward
slides.text: Block B · topological order A topological order puts every edge forward The jobs in the order they are peeled form a topological order: for every edge (u, v), u comes before v. The morning of five tasks has 4 of them: ABCDE, ABCED, BACDE, BACED. An order is rarely unique. Order A C B D E: edge Positions Forward? A → C 1, 2 yes B → C 3, 2 no C → D 2, 4 yes C → E 2, 5 yes Check, do not trust. The definition is edge by edge: one backward edge makes an order invalid, and no backward edge, with every node once, makes it valid.

slides.title: A loop invariant proves the peeled order is topological
slides.text: Why peeling is correct A loop invariant proves the peeled order is topological Part For the invariant "every job in the list has all its predecessors earlier in the list" Initialisation The list is empty: nothing to check Maintenance A job is added only when all its predecessors are already in the list Termination If every job is peeled, the invariant covers every edge: the list is a topological order

slides.title: Which order is valid?
slides.text: Checkpoint Which order is valid? Edges: P → R, Q → R, R → S, Q → S. Which running order respects every edge? P R Q S Q P S R Q P R S R Q P S

slides.title: Count paths into a node from the counts into its predecessors
slides.text: Block C · recurrences Count paths into a node from the counts into its predecessors In a grid walked right or down, the paths into a point are the paths into the point above plus the paths into the point on the left: P(i, j) = P(i − 1, j) + P(i, j − 1), with 1 along the edges. 1 1 1 1 2 3 1 3 6 Why it works Every path into a point arrives by exactly one last edge, so the paths split into disjoint groups, one per predecessor: the sum rule of week 5. Walk the points in a topological order so each sum uses finished counts.

slides.title: Counts that look small at n = 10 are out of reach at n = 30
slides.text: Growth Counts that look small at n = 10 are out of reach at n = 30 n n² 2ⁿ n! 10 100 1,024 3.6 × 10⁶ 20 400 1,048,576 2.4 × 10¹⁸ 30 900 1,073,741,824 2.7 × 10³² Paths across an n by n grid: 252 at n = 5, 184,756 at n = 10, about 1.2 × 10¹⁷ at n = 30 Listing every path or order is fine for a toy and hopeless at scale A recurrence does one step per node: count without listing

slides.title: Guess a closed form from the first values, then prove it by induction
slides.text: Solve, then prove Guess a closed form from the first values, then prove it by induction 1 · Recurrence Links among n people: H(1) = 0, H(n) = H(n − 1) + (n − 1) → 2 · Guess 0, 1, 3, 6, 10: H(n) = n(n − 1)/2 → 3 · Prove H(n − 1) + (n − 1) = (n − 1)(n − 2)/2 + (n − 1) = n(n − 1)/2 Takeaway. The step uses the hypothesis for n − 1: that is the induction. Test the guess in code first, as the capstone asks.

slides.title: What does the recurrence give?
slides.text: Checkpoint What does the recurrence give? H(1) = 0 and H(n) = H(n − 1) + (n − 1). What is H(6)? 21 30 36 15

slides.title: The portfolio rubric
slides.text: How the portfolio is scored The portfolio rubric Claims stated precisely 15% Test code before each proof, limits stated 20% Each proof valid: every step justified 30% The induction proof complete 20% Readable, reproducible, AI use recorded 15% Test first, then prove. A passing test is evidence for the cases it ran; only the proof covers the rest.

slides.title: 10 minutes for each defence
slides.text: Format 10 minutes for each defence 1 · The claim The assessor picks one of your three proofs. State the claim and the method you chose. About one minute. 2 · Step by step Walk through the proof and say why each step holds, then what your tests showed. About six minutes. 3 · A changed hypothesis The assessor changes one assumption. Say whether the proof survives and which step breaks. About three minutes. Peer dry run. Pairs defend one proof to each other and change one hypothesis for each other. The partner writes one strength, one question and one suggestion.
